purpose: Put a MEASURED number against kg0, which the project lists among its unfitted constants and names as the largest single source of uncertainty in the hydrate results.

measured_constant.source: Englezos, P., Kalogerakis, N., Dholabhai, P.D., Bishnoi, P.R. (1987), 'Kinetics of formation of methane and ethane gas hydrates', Chem. Eng. Sci. 42(11):2647-2658; and the companion mixtures paper 42(11):2659-2666.
measured_constant.conditions: Semi-batch stirred tank, 274-282 K, 0.636-8.903 MPa. Above ~400 rpm the mass-transfer resistance around the particles is eliminated, so this is the REACTION constant, not an effective one. It is the constant the Kim-Bishnoi model uses.
measured_constant.provenance: Value confirmed from multiple independent citing sources; the primary paper is paywalled and was NOT read directly. Treat as a literature-quoted constant, not a first-hand transcription.

conversion_to_model_units.why: Englezos drives growth with a FUGACITY difference and reports a molar flux per unit hydrate area. This model drives it with SUBCOOLING and reports a linear growth velocity. Converting needs the slope of the hydrate curve and the hydrate volume per mole of enclathrated gas.
conversion_to_model_units.curve_slope: dP_eq/dT from THIS repository's own refitted correlation (T_eq = 0.45897 ln(P)^2 + 5.74157 ln(P) - 22.94667), so the conversion is consistent with the solver rather than a textbook curve: 6.32 bar/K at 60 bar, 10.03 at 100, 14.51 at 150.
conversion_to_model_units.hydrate_basis: sI, 5.75 H2O per CH4, rho_hyd = 920 kg/m3 (the case's own value) -> 1.299e-4 m3 per mol gas.
conversion_to_model_units.fugacity_assumption: f ~ P. The methane fugacity coefficient is ~0.85 at 100 bar and 10 C, so this OVERSTATES the driving force by ~15 % and therefore understates the implied kg0 by the same factor. Not corrected, because it does not change the order of magnitude that the comparison turns on.

model_value.at: dTsub_ref_C = 1.0, growth_exp_n = 1.5 (was 1.0 when this reconciliation was first made). kg0 is unchanged by that move and so is this comparison: Englezos' rate is FIRST-ORDER in the fugacity difference, so it constrains the COEFFICIENT kg0 and says nothing about the subcooling exponent. The exponent is anchored separately -- see kinetics_subcooling_exponent_literature.json.

finding: The model's kg0 is ~800x the intrinsic constant at 100 bar. That is NOT a discrepancy of 800x in predicted rate, because the two multiply DIFFERENT AREAS. Rate = k * A * driving force. Englezos' K* multiplies hydrate PARTICLE surface in a stirred slurry, whose specific area is commonly 1e2-1e4 m2/m3; this model's kg0 multiplies a_wall = 4/D scaled by liquid holdup and water fraction, which is 14.6 m2/m3 at a 10.75 in bore. A smaller area needs a larger coefficient for the same physical rate, and the ratio of areas spans the ratio of constants.
what_this_establishes: kg0 = 6.0e-7 m/s is consistent in ORDER OF MAGNITUDE with measured intrinsic kinetics once the area basis is reconciled. It is no longer a number with nothing behind it.
what_this_does_NOT_establish: It is not a fit, and it does not pin kg0. Closing the remaining factor needs the specific area the slurry kinetics were measured against, which the citing sources do not give, and a measurement of the wall-deposit area in a real line. n and C_phi are untouched by this: Englezos' rate is first-order in the fugacity difference, which supports growth_exp_n = 1 as a FORM but says nothing about a subcooling exponent, and C_phi has no measured counterpart in this literature at all.

area_basis_CLOSED.was: The residual factor of ~800 between the assumed kg0 and the measured intrinsic constant was attributed to the area basis, but the particle area Englezos reduced against was not carried by any citing source, so the factor stayed open.
area_basis_CLOSED.source: Clarke, M.A. and Bishnoi, P.R. improved the Englezos model using IN-SITU particle size analysis: a Lasentec focused beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) probe measuring particle chord lengths between 0.5 and 100 um in a semi-batch stirred-tank reactor. The gas consumption rate in that model is proportional to the SECOND MOMENT of the particle size distribution, i.e. to total particle surface area.

reconciliation.formula: a_wall = 4/D * alpha_l * water_fraction, D = 0.2545 m, alpha_l = 0.45, wc = 0.70
reconciliation.reactor_particle_area: phi * 6/d for spheres of diameter d at hydrate volume fraction phi
reconciliation.verdict: For any plausible hydrate volume fraction in a semi-batch stirred reactor (1-5 %), the assumed kg0 implies an Englezos particle diameter of 15-76 um. That is INSIDE the 0.5-100 um range the FBRM probe measures and typical of hydrate slurries. The 800x is therefore accounted for by geometry, not left as a discrepancy.

area_basis_CLOSED.status: CLOSED to a quantitative consistency AND the consistency has now survived a falsification test against an independent measured particle-size distribution. Tightness: about one order of magnitude, limited by whether primary particles or agglomerates set the reacting area.
area_basis_CLOSED.what_would_refute_it: A measured hydrate particle diameter in that reactor near 1 um or near 1 mm. At 1 um the implied kg0 would be ~15x smaller than assumed; at 1 mm, ~13x larger. The reconciliation is a prediction about particle size, and it is falsifiable by the same FBRM measurement that supplied the range.
area_basis_CLOSED.residual_caveat: SUPERSEDED by a measurement, and one number in it was wrong. The FBRM chord-length range was recorded here as 0.5-100 um; the instrument's limits are 0.5 to 1000 um. More importantly the caveat said the range bounded rather than pinned the particle size, because no citing source carried a measured mean. One does -- see prediction_tested_against_a_measurement below.

prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.the_prediction: The reconciliation is not a fit; it is a PREDICTION about particle size. For a hydrate volume fraction of 1-5 % in a stirred reactor, kg0 = 6.0e-7 m/s implies an Englezos particle diameter of 15-76 um. The file's own falsification condition was a measured diameter 'near 1 um or near 1 mm'.
prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.the_measurement: Open-access FBRM measurements on a hydrate slurry give a MEAN CHORD LENGTH of 9-10 um before hydrate formation, rising to 15-40 um after it, with the square-weighted chord length moving from 25-35 um to 150-300 um and the large-particle population from 10-100 um to 100-400 um.
prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.source: Study on the blockage mechanism of carbon dioxide hydrate slurry and its microscopic particle characteristics, PMC9088890 (open access). FBRM CLD limits 0.5-1000 um, error +/-0.2 um.
prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.verdict: THE PREDICTION SURVIVES. A measured mean chord length of 15-40 um for hydrate particles falls inside the predicted 15-76 um, and is neither of the two values that would have refuted it. Converting chord length to diameter makes the agreement no worse: for spheres the mean chord is 2/3 of the diameter, so 15-40 um chord implies 22-60 um diameter, still inside the band.
prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.the_counter_consideration_that_survives: The SQUARE-WEIGHTED chord length after formation is 150-300 um and the large-particle population reaches 400 um. If the reacting area is set by AGGLOMERATES rather than by primary particles, the specific area is several times smaller and the implied kg0 correspondingly larger -- by roughly the ratio of 150-300 um to 15-40 um, so a factor of 4-10. That does not refute the reconciliation but it does bound how tight it is: consistent to within about an order of magnitude, not to a factor of two.
prediction_tested_against_a_measurement.system_mismatch_stated: This is CO2 hydrate in a flow loop, not methane in Englezos' semi-batch stirred reactor. It is an independent measurement of the same physical quantity in a related system, not a measurement of Englezos' own particles, and is used as a plausibility test of a predicted size rather than as a transcription of his area basis.
